systems.name: Five-Zone Fretboard Navigation System
systems.summary: The book's central spatial system organizes the guitar fretboard into five vertical zones, each anchored by a guide chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7), enabling the player to 'visualize vertically but play horizontally.' Zones are not visited in sequence; instead, the player skips adjacent zones to preserve left-right hand synchronization. Zone transitions require a non-standard 4-1-4-1 finger alternation and must be executed at the 1st or 6th string to avoid picking-direction conflicts. Guide chords function as navigational landmarks rather than harmonic instructions. The system applies uniformly across pentatonic scales (Chapter 3), blues scales (Chapter 4), and the natural major/minor scales (Chapter 6), making it the book's universal fretboard-organization framework.

members.name: Zone 1
members.summary: First vertical zone of the fretboard, anchored by a guide chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7 voicing in that position).

members.name: Zone 2
members.summary: Second vertical zone; typically skipped when traversing from Zone 1 to preserve hand synchronization.

members.name: Zone 3
members.summary: Third vertical zone; the default destination when skipping from Zone 1.

members.name: Zone 4
members.summary: Fourth vertical zone.

members.name: Zone 5
members.summary: Fifth vertical zone, completing coverage of the full fretboard range.

members.name: Cmaj7 Guide Chord Shape
members.summary: Chord shape used as navigational anchor for Ionian-side zones.

members.name: Am7 Guide Chord Shape
members.summary: Chord shape used as navigational anchor for Aeolian-side zones.

traversal_rules.name: Zone-Skip Rule
traversal_rules.summary: When moving from one zone to another, skip the immediately adjacent zone (e.g., from Zone 1 go to Zone 3) to preserve the connection between both hands.

references.topic: Skipping zones to preserve hand connection
references.quote_excerpt: we must skip the 2nd zone thus going to the 3rd zone...otherwise the connection between both hands would be lost

traversal_rules.name: 1st/6th String Zone-Change Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Zone transitions using alternate picking are cleanest when executed at the 1st or 6th string; other string boundaries introduce picking-direction hazards.

references.quote_excerpt: pentatonic connections with alternate picking work perfectly when we use the 1st or 6th string to change from one zone to another

traversal_rules.name: 4-1-4-1 Zone-Transition Fingering
traversal_rules.summary: When crossing zone boundaries, use the non-standard 4-1 finger alternation rather than conventional sequential fingering.

references.quote_excerpt: when we change from one zone to another we have a non common type of fingering (4, 1, 4, 1, 4, 1 and 4, 1)

traversal_rules.name: String-Change Upstroke Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Every time a string change occurs, the preceding stroke must be an upstroke to maintain picking-hand/fretting-hand synchronization.

references.topic: string change requires up stroke rule
references.quote_excerpt: everytime we want to change from one string to another, we should play an up stroke

traversal_rules.name: Guide-Chord Zone Anchoring
traversal_rules.summary: Each zone is associated with a fixed chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7) that anchors memory for that zone's root position; the chord root guides navigation, not harmony.

references.quote_excerpt: Each zone will be related with a chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7). The chords will guide us
they are only to guide us into the 5 zones, nothing else

traversal_rules.name: Horizontal-Over-Vertical Play Preference
traversal_rules.summary: After using vertical zone visualization to orient position, melodic lines should connect zones horizontally rather than remaining locked within a single vertical zone.

references.quote_excerpt: we visualize vertically but play horizontally most of the time
Usually, the vertical ideas do not work as well as the horizontal ideas

modification_rules.name: Two-Notes-Per-String Vertical Fingering
modification_rules.summary: Pentatonic scale zones are fingered with exactly two notes per string to enable clean vertical playing within each zone.

references.quote_excerpt: pentatonic scales work perfectly when played vertically because they can be played using two notes per string

modification_rules.name: Note-Count-Per-String Picking Direction Modifier
modification_rules.summary: The number of notes played on each string determines the picking direction for that string, and any change to fingering that alters this count must be accompanied by a corresponding picking adjustment.

references.topic: notes per string affects picking direction
references.quote_excerpt: the number of notes we play per string...can completely change the right hand picking, destroying the connection between both hands

systems.name: Chord Arpeggio Construction System
systems.summary: This system organizes all triad and tetrad arpeggios by root-string group (5th string vs. 6th string) with three shapes per group, and extends to inverted arpeggios visualized relative to a guide root. The system's traversal logic covers how to move between arpeggio shapes using guide-root selection, and its modification rules govern transposition (replacing open strings with the first finger) and the distinction between ascending arpeggios (which define fretboard zones) and descending arpeggios (which typically span two zones). In Chapter 7, the system is extended to 'Major 7th and Minor 7th Scale Arpeggios' — descending Cmaj7 and Am7 arpeggios with added color tones — as the principal device for navigating the avoid note over the I and VIm chords.

members.name: 5th-String Root Group
members.summary: Arpeggios whose root note falls on the 5th string; contains three distinct shapes for triads and tetrads.

members.name: 6th-String Root Group
members.summary: Arpeggios whose root note falls on the 6th string; contains three distinct shapes for triads and tetrads.

members.name: Triad Arpeggio
members.summary: Three-note chord arpeggio (root, 3rd, 5th) played melodically from root position.

members.name: Tetrad Arpeggio (7th Chord Arpeggio)
members.summary: Four-note chord arpeggio including the 7th, played melodically from root position.

members.name: Inverted Arpeggio
members.summary: Arpeggio whose bass note is not the root; visualized relative to a guide root on either the 5th or 6th string.

members.name: Major 7th Scale Arpeggio (with Added Notes)
members.summary: Descending Cmaj7 arpeggio with added color tones, derived from Benson solos, used to avoid the perfect 4th over Imaj7.

members.name: Minor 7th Scale Arpeggio (with Added Notes)
members.summary: Descending Am7 arpeggio with added color tones, used to avoid the flat 6th over VIm7.

traversal_rules.name: Guide-Root Selection Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Select the 5th-string or 6th-string guide root to determine which arpeggio visualization applies for a given fretboard position.

references.quote_excerpt: The inverted arpeggios can be visualized many ways, depending on the guide root we

traversal_rules.name: Ascending Arpeggio Zone Definition Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Ascending arpeggios establish and define the current fretboard zone; descending arpeggios characteristically span two zones.

references.quote_excerpt: ascending arpeggios will define the fretboard zones, because the descending arpeggios will almost always use two zones

modification_rules.name: Open-String First-Finger Transposition Rule
modification_rules.summary: When transposing an arpeggio shape out of open position, replace each open string with the first finger to preserve the shape's interval relationships.

references.topic: Open strings replaceable by first finger
references.quote_excerpt: all the open strings...finger number [1 can replace them when transposing]

modification_rules.name: Added-Note Color Tone Rule (Scale Arpeggios)
modification_rules.summary: Descending Cmaj7 and Am7 scale arpeggios are augmented with color tones derived from transcribed Benson solos, yielding lines that fit Ionian/Lydian and Dorian/Aeolian contexts while avoiding the perfect 4th.

references.quote_excerpt: Cmaj7 and Am7 descending chord arpeggios with added notes

references.topic: Two chords focus — solving avoid note
references.quote_excerpt: we will create melodies for Cmaj7 that can fit over Ionian or Lydian chords, and melodies for Am7 that can fit over Dorian or Aeolian chords

modification_rules.name: Guitar Arpeggiation Constraint for Superimposition
modification_rules.summary: Because stacked chords cannot be voiced simultaneously on guitar (as they can on piano), superimposed harmonies must be realized by arpeggiation of each chord in sequence.

references.topic: Chord stacking on guitar vs piano
references.quote_excerpt: it is difficult to play these superimposed chords correctly on the guitar...we must arpeggiate two chords

modification_rules.name: Three-Finger Playing Preference (No Fourth Finger)
modification_rules.summary: Arpeggio and scale fingerings preferentially use three fingers, avoiding the fourth finger, following Benson's characteristic left-hand approach.

references.quote_excerpt: he does not use the pinky or 4th finger very often, playing mostly with three fingers

systems.name: Blues Scale Combination System
systems.summary: This system governs how the minor blues scale and major blues scale are combined within a key to produce authentic blues improvisation. The two scales are not interchangeable: the minor blues scale can summarize all chords in a major or minor blues form, but when the two scales are mixed, the player must follow harmony chord-by-chord rather than collapsing all changes into one scale. The major blues scale (derived from the 3rd degree of the minor blues scale) applies over major chords including dominant 7ths, but sounds most bluesy only in combination with the minor blues scale. Overreliance on either scale alone is explicitly named a failure mode ('lazy' improvising). The system also inherits the five-zone navigation structure, requiring at least two zones for horizontal melodic ideas.

members.name: Minor Blues Scale
members.summary: Minor pentatonic plus the blue note (b5); can be used across all chords of a major or minor blues form as a single summarizing scale.

members.name: Major Blues Scale
members.summary: Same pitches as the minor blues scale but starting from the 3rd degree; applies over individual major chords including dominant 7ths.

members.name: Eb Major Blues Scale (Minor Tonality Pairing)
members.summary: In minor tonality, the minor blues scale in C pairs with the Eb major blues scale rather than the C major blues scale.

traversal_rules.name: Chord-by-Chord Scale Following Rule
traversal_rules.summary: When mixing minor and major blues scales, do not summarize all chord changes into one scale; instead, assign each scale to its appropriate chord or chord type individually.

references.quote_excerpt: we cannot summarize all the chords into one scale anymore, we must follow the harmony

traversal_rules.name: Two-Zone Minimum for Horizontal Lines
traversal_rules.summary: Horizontal blues-scale melodic ideas must connect at least two zones to function properly.

references.quote_excerpt: we must use at least two zones to make it work

modification_rules.name: Minor Blues over Dominant 7th — Major 3rd Caveat
modification_rules.summary: When using the minor blues scale over a dominant 7th chord, the major 3rd must be played quickly in the phrase to avoid harmonic clash.

references.quote_excerpt: Make sure to play the major 3rd quickly in the phrase, otherwise the melody can sound wrong

modification_rules.name: Blues Scale Combination Restricted to Major Tonality
modification_rules.summary: The same-key minor+major blues combination rule applies only to major tonalities; in minor tonality, the minor blues in C pairs with the Eb major blues scale instead.

references.topic: Combining blues scales for bluesy sound
references.quote_excerpt: Blues scales played in the same key work only for major tonalities and not for minor

modification_rules.name: Single-Scale Overreliance Prohibition
modification_rules.summary: Relying on any single blues scale for the entirety of an improvisation produces lazy, stagnant lines; the system requires combination of multiple melodic ideas.

references.quote_excerpt: Be careful not to rely on this technique. It will make you sound like a lazy improviser.
the secret of a great improviser is to combine all the melodic ideas at once

systems.name: Superimposition and Improvisational Vocabulary System
systems.summary: This system governs how the player builds, stores, and deploys improvisational vocabulary through a language-learning loop: listen to great soloists, sing their lines, transcribe them, then extract the underlying harmonic concept to generate new lines rather than simply reproducing copied licks. The vocabulary units (licks) are treated as fixed melodic-plus-physical units — pitch sequence, fingering, and picking are inseparable. Superimposition is defined as the melodic or harmonic joining of two or more chords; on guitar this requires arpeggiation because simultaneous chord-stacking is unavailable. Rhythmic displacement — offsetting intervallic patterns with rhythmic motifs — prevents mechanical predictability when applying arpeggio-based patterns. The system explicitly requires parallel study of volumes 1 and 2 for the rhythmic vocabulary needed to vary lines with taste.

members.name: Lick (Pre-Set Melodic-Physical Unit)
members.summary: A fixed small melodic idea with inseparable fingering and picking; the basic vocabulary unit of improvisation, learned by singing before playing.

members.name: Minor Blues Substitution Trick
members.summary: Context-specific substitution vocabulary required because minor blues mixes minor and dominant chord types that a single pentatonic does not cleanly summarize.

members.name: Descending Scale Arpeggio with Added Notes
members.summary: Zone-by-zone descending Cmaj7/Am7 arpeggios with color tones, the primary superimposition device for I and VIm chords.

members.name: Intervallic Pattern with Rhythmic Displacement
members.summary: An intervallic arpeggio-based melodic pattern made musical by applying rhythmic motifs and motif-overlap (starting each motif by repeating the last note of the previous).

members.name: Superimposed Chord Pair
members.summary: Two chords joined melodically or harmonically; realized on guitar through sequential arpeggiation rather than simultaneous voicing.

traversal_rules.name: Language-Learning Transcription Loop
traversal_rules.summary: Move from listening to singing to transcribing to concept-extraction to new-line generation, cycling through solos of great artists to build vocabulary that transcends imitation.

references.topic: Purpose of the book — transcend transcription
references.quote_excerpt: understand, organize and transcend what we transcribe finding out the musical concepts behind them

references.topic: Music as language — listen and copy
references.quote_excerpt: Music is exactly like a language...listen and copy from the greatest artists we love

traversal_rules.name: Context-Driven Lick/Fingering Selection
traversal_rules.summary: When applying a lick, choose fingering and picking options based on the surrounding fretboard position (where you are coming from or going to).

references.quote_excerpt: You can choose one of the examples depending on where you are coming from or going to on the guitar fretboard

traversal_rules.name: Minor Pentatonic Family Preference Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Lick lines built purely from minor pentatonic (without major pentatonic mixture) are preferentially deployed over chords belonging to the minor chord family, though the rule is not absolute.

references.topic: Pure minor pentatonic over minor family
references.quote_excerpt: our preference is to use the lines over minor chords or chord sequences belonging to the minor chord family
This is not a rule. Melodic lines using only the minor pentatonic scale will often work perfectly over major chords

modification_rules.name: Singing-First Internalization Rule
modification_rules.summary: Every lick or melodic line must be sung and aurally internalized before physical application; ear and body memory precede theoretical understanding.

references.quote_excerpt: learn to sing every melodic line (lick) that you know. Internalize the sound.
we must learn to sing melodies of songs and solos of our favorite artists

modification_rules.name: Memorize-Before-Theory Substitution Rule
modification_rules.summary: Minor blues substitution tricks must be memorized as vocabulary before their underlying theory is understood; pragmatic fluency precedes theoretical comprehension.

references.quote_excerpt: it is not necessary to understand the theory behind it, just memorize them
the minor blues form has two different types of chords (minor and dominant), so we must learn some substitution tricks

modification_rules.name: Rhythmic Displacement Anti-Predictability Rule
modification_rules.summary: Every intervallic arpeggio pattern must be offset with rhythmic motifs (rhythmic displacement) and motif-overlap to prevent mechanical, predictable sounding lines.

references.quote_excerpt: Every intervallic pattern should be applied using them...what we call rhythmic displacement
DO NOT rely on these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring.

modification_rules.name: Fixed Fingering-and-Picking Lick Unit Rule
modification_rules.summary: A lick's notated fingering and picking are inseparable from the lick itself and must be followed exactly; they are not arbitrary but are chosen for hand coordination.

references.topic: Fingering & picking must be followed exactly
references.quote_excerpt: follow the given fingering and picking possibilities exactly as notated for each one of the examples
Play the exact suggested fingering...They were chosen specifically to better help you master this technique

modification_rules.name: Pattern Note-Order Invariant
modification_rules.summary: Within any melodic pattern, the sequence of pitches is fixed; only the rhythm applied to that sequence may vary.

references.quote_excerpt: the order of the notes is always the same, the only thing that changes is the rhythm, otherwise we would be changing the melodic pattern

modification_rules.name: Avoid-Note Omission over Imaj7 and VIm7
modification_rules.summary: The perfect 4th (over Ionian/Imaj7) and flat 6th (over Aeolian/VIm7) are omitted as default choices; they may be retained in exceptional musical contexts.

references.quote_excerpt: Be careful with the avoid notes of both scales (perfect 4th in the Ionian mode, and flat 6th in the Aeolian mode)
there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation

references.topic: The Secret of the Two Chords — premise
references.quote_excerpt: the avoid note (perfect 4th) can create some melodic problems, especially over the root chord and the relative minor chord (Cmaj7 and Am7)
